excerpt_original: Women’s bodies, scars and sisterhood in the new film from the director of “Next Sohee”, with Kim Do-yeon and Ando Sakura

blocks.text: Dora (2026) by July Jung Film Review
Women’s bodies, scars and sisterhood in the new film from the director of “Next Sohee”, with Kim Do-yeon and Ando Sakura

The much-loved Korean director July Jung , the mind behind “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and, more recently, “Next Sohee” (2022), returns to directing a female lead in “Dora”, which premiered at the Cannes Film Festival and arrives on home soil in the Gala section of the Busan International Film Festival.
Dora is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The film tells the story of Dora (Kim Do-yeon), a teenager whose distress and trauma manifest in a troublesome skin condition. Her skin seems to rot in the face of life’s stresses, and Dora becomes keenly aware that this outbreak is driven by an inner turmoil. Her mother and father, in the midst of a crisis, decide to retreat to a small house by the sea to bring some comfort to their marriage and to their daughter. The neighbors are old friends of the father’s, with two lively twins who immediately treat Dora as their big sister.

Dora exerts a magnetic pull on everyone who crosses her path, to the point that the positive energies of this extended family help her heal. The couple of friends in particular benefit: Yeon-su (Song Sae-byeok) takes up painting again and wants her as a model, while Mina (Sakura Ando) goes out of her way to make her feel less out of place, well aware of how hard it can be to fit in. Just when Dora seems to have finally found a balance, the crystal castle begins to crack, and those who had rejoiced in her presence no longer seem to consider her welcome.

July Jung has a wealth of experience in telling stories of women and complex female portraits, where shadows and light alternate. In her previous, acclaimed work, “Next Sohee” (2022), she portrayed adolescence as a gradual passage, giving voice to young people misunderstood by adults. Dora at first seems to show us a different world, one of affable, welcoming adults. But that welcome suddenly turns into selfishness. And not only that: truth and lies wear the same face and warp themselves to suit personal convenience.

The director’s intention is plain: not to offer a complete resolution to the crisis of the two gracious female figures she focuses on, namely Kim Do-yeon’s Dora on one side and Sakura Ando’s Mina on the other. Both are misfits, misunderstood victims of different forms of exile. Dora, masterfully drawn, is a teenager who has had to withdraw from the system, suspended as if she were a ghost; when she arrives at the summer house, she drags herself along, surviving, hidden and shy of the sun and the sea. Few words, eyes lowered; every inch of her exposed skin is experienced as a risk and a weakness.

Mina, Japanese by birth, has had to give up her profession and her life because of an illness that, like Dora, has left her scarred. In Korea, she withdraws into the greenery because nature soothes her pain. Outside her vegetable garden, she does not belong: not to the family, not to the place, and this sense of suspension binds her to the newly arrived girl. Ando gives us first a woman who shows her scar with resignation, marked by physical and mental alienation; and then, when she discovers she can reclaim the body she had forgotten, she does so with joy and avidity.

Yet society does not seem to grant full rehabilitation to those who have lost their beauty: they are “empty shells,” as her husband calls her, a stranger by now, with whom she is forced to live with. It is in sisterhood, then, that sincere comfort is found.

The husbands in the film, though perfectly integrated, are incapable of understanding, processing, accepting and fighting for their bonds. When a relationship ages, they look for something else. Dora watches in astonishment as they seek to renew themselves at the expense of those who stand beside them. Dora is accused of being the destructive, destabilising element, but hers is a revealing force. She unmasks the lie and bombards the foundations of falsehood. And yet it is almost painful to watch how she takes pity and feels responsible even in the face of abuse, making plain the psychological pressure she is under.

Cinematographer Irina Lubtchansky condenses the protagonist’s emotional life through sharp chiaroscuro that opens up to saturated colors as her slow, gradual healing progresses. The viewer feels the closure and introspection of the moments of crisis, and the openness and connection with the environment and the outside world when Dora lives more joyful moments. The editing too tends to disappear, making the passing of time felt less in step with the protagonist’s happiness, which thus becomes the spark of the whole work.

Alongside the main drama, July Jung sets small interludes of childlike tenderness, youthful jealousy and sunny summer liberation. The film thus approaches the darkest and hardest-to-process part without too much heaviness, leaving the audience the right breath to return to suffering over the wounds of young Dora’s emaciated body, covered in sores. The setting is also a fundamental component, underlining the division between these worlds that at first do not belong together, and then end up blending.

Dora’s family home is designer architecture, but cold and unwelcoming; Mina’s home, by contrast, is lively, lit by warm lights, colored by her husband’s paintings and by the lush vegetable garden that yields fruit despite the torrential rain. It goes without saying that the two women’s clothing becomes their human icon, and that young Dora’s transformation as she blossoms into adulthood corresponds to a shift in her wardrobe toward lightness and carefree ease. And so her skin, once concealed, becomes a new garment to wear and display with pride and pleasure.

Despite some narrative slowdowns that pull us away from a thrilling protagonist we never wish to leave, “Dora” manages to offer a stimulating dialogue between two complex femininities, thanks to truly successful casting choices. Kim Do-yeon and Sakura Ando are two opposite poles that attract at first and explode in collision: once we focus on the uniqueness of these two portraits, the partial fog lying at the edges of the story tends to lift.
